title: Bored or boring? Adjectives
goal: Choose -ed or -ing adjectives, and put adjectives in the right place
intro: Adjectives describe nouns. In English they come before the noun (“a quiet street”) or after verbs like be, look, feel, seem (“the street is quiet”). They never take a plural -s. Two adjective families confuse many learners: -ed words describe how you feel, and -ing words describe what causes the feeling.

rules.rule: -ed = how a person feels. -ing = the thing that causes it.
examples: I was bored. The lecture was boring.
She is interested in art. Art is interesting.

rules.rule: After look, feel, seem, sound, taste, smell: use an adjective, not -ly.

mistakes.why: The movie causes the feeling: exciting.

ex.q: I was really ___ by the news.

ex.y: The trip caused the feeling: tiring.

ex.q: I'm so exciting about the trip!
ex.fixed: I'm so excited about the trip!

ex.y: The meeting caused the feeling: confusing.

ex.q: I get ___ when people are late. (annoyed / annoying)

ex.a: The last episode was really disappointing.
ex.y: The episode caused the feeling: disappointing.

ex.q: Correct this: “I was very boring in the class.”
a: I was very bored in the class
I was very bored in class

talk: Talk about a film or series you watched recently. Was it boring or interesting? How did you feel? Use at least three -ed and -ing adjectives.
